title: One layer up from Day 1
lead: Day 1 put a model inside a system. Day 2 puts it inside a loop that acts.
cues: Day 1: a one-way path from records to a business decision.
Day 2: the model chooses an action, not just a score.
The return arrow is new: results flow back as context.
Same engineering question: what must surround the model?
takeaway: An agent is still a model inside an architecture — now one that loops.
source: Day 1 lecture · Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §1

title: Agent = model + harness
lead: The harness is everything except the model. A source-code study of eleven harnesses found the same seven subsystems in all of them.
cues: Agent loop at the centre: model → tool → observation.
Six more subsystems: LLM access, tools, safety, memory, orchestration, extensions.
Every harness takes a position on all seven, even if it is “none”.
Interfaces sit on top: terminal, editors, chat gateways.
takeaway: The harness is the part you can engineer.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §2.3, Table 1

title: Eleven harnesses, from one tool to 109
lead: The same seven subsystems, built with tool surfaces that differ by two orders of magnitude.
cues: Minimal end: Mini-SWE-Agent works through one bash tool; Pi exposes four by default.
Maximal end: Hermes registers 69 tools and scopes them per platform; OpenClaw ships 109.
More code is not better results: loop sophistication does not predict benchmark performance.
Most code goes elsewhere: safety, user experience, extensibility and clients.
takeaway: Tool count is a design philosophy, not a quality score.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §5 Table 4, §8.1 Fig. 3

title: The agent loop: decide, act, observe
lead: One cycle repeats until the model answers in text instead of calling a tool.
cues: The context window accumulates state: every pass writes into it.
Clockwise: model → permission gate → tool → observation.
Steering input waits for a safe boundary, never mid-tool-call.
Stop conditions differ: no cap in Pi, a 90-step budget in Hermes.
takeaway: A loop with a growing context — everything else manages that loop.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §6

title: Pi: a minimal core, everything else an extension
lead: Pi keeps the core small and moves safety, sub-agents and plan mode into extensions.
cues: Four layers: interfaces → product → loop → model gateway.
Session tree: JSONL entries you can fork and rewind.
Extension host: sub-agents, plan mode and permissions hook into the event stream.
Trade-off: a small core, but safety depends on what you install.
takeaway: Minimal core plus extensions is one coherent harness architecture.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §10–12 · Zechner (2025); Pi docs, github.com/earendil-works/pi

title: What eleven harnesses share — and lack
lead: Production harnesses converge on skills and context files, and all skip two popular technologies.
cues: Shared: skills, summarised history, Markdown context files, MCP.
Absent everywhere: agentic frameworks and embedding search over code.
Instead: hand-rolled async loops and deterministic search (grep, LSP).
Next: a vocabulary for the agent inside the loop.
takeaway: The field runs on simple loops and deterministic retrieval.
source: Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, §13.2, Observation 8–9
